summary.text: Write \(n=2^a m\) with \(m\) odd, and split the odd divisors below \(\sqrt{2n}\) according as \(m\le 2^{a+1}d^2\) or not: removing the power-of-two part bijects the first class with the middle divisors, while \(d\mapsto m/d\) bijects the second class with the odd divisors above \(\sqrt{2n}\). Thus the number of low odd divisors equals the number of middle divisors plus the number of high odd divisors; since all odd divisors split into low and high classes, subtracting the middle count leaves twice the high count.

full_proof.text:
Let \(n\) be a positive integer. We shall prove that
\[
\#\{d:d\mid n,\ d\text{ odd}\}
-
\#\{c:c\mid n,\ n\le 2c^2,\ c^2<2n\}
=
2\#\{e:e\mid n,\ e\text{ odd},\ 2n<e^2\}.
\]
The condition \(n\le 2c^2\) and \(c^2<2n\) is precisely
\[
\sqrt{n/2}\le c<\sqrt{2n},
\]
so the second count on the left is the number of middle divisors. Likewise, for positive \(e\), the inequality \(2n<e^2\) says \(e>\sqrt{2n}\). Thus this identity is exactly the stated conjecture.

Write
\[
n=2^a m,
\]
where \(a\ge 0\) and \(m\) is odd. Thus \(m\) is the odd part of \(n\), and
\[
2n=2^{a+1}m. \tag{1}
\]
We will use repeatedly the elementary fact that the odd divisors of \(n\) are exactly the divisors of \(m\). Indeed, every divisor of \(m\) is odd and divides \(n=2^am\). Conversely, if an odd integer \(d\) divides \(2^am\), then \(d\) is relatively prime to \(2^a\), so Euclid's lemma gives \(d\mid m\).

Define the following finite sets:
\[
\begin{aligned}
O&=\{d:d\mid n,\ d\text{ odd}\},\\
L&=\{d:d\mid n,\ d\text{ odd},\ d^2<2n\},\\
G&=\{d:d\mid n,\ d\text{ odd},\ 2n<d^2\},\\
M&=\{c:c\mid n,\ n\le 2c^2,\ c^2<2n\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(O\) is the set of odd divisors, \(G\) is the set whose cardinality occurs on the right-hand side, and \(M\) is the set of middle divisors.

First, \(O\) is the disjoint union of \(L\) and \(G\). To see that no third case occurs, observe that an odd \(d\) has odd square, whereas \(2n\) is even. Hence \(d^2\ne 2n\). Therefore every odd divisor satisfies exactly one of \(d^2<2n\) and \(2n<d^2\), and consequently
\[
|O|=|L|+|G|. \tag{2}
\]

The main part of the proof is the second counting identity
\[
|L|=|M|+|G|. \tag{3}
\]
To establish it, partition \(L\) into the two sets
\[
\begin{aligned}
A&=\{d\in L:m\le 2^{a+1}d^2\},\\
B&=\{d\in L:2^{a+1}d^2<m\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
These are complementary subsets of \(L\), so
\[
|L|=|A|+|B|. \tag{4}
\]
We shall construct a bijection between \(M\) and \(A\), and another between \(B\) and \(G\).

First consider a middle divisor \(c\in M\). Factor out its full power of \(2\): write uniquely
\[
c=2^b d,
\]
where \(b\ge 0\) and \(d\) is odd. Since \(c\mid n=2^am\), we have \(b\le a\), and the odd part \(d\) divides \(m\), hence also divides \(n\). Moreover \(d\le c\), so the upper middle-divisor inequality gives
\[
d^2\le c^2<2n. \tag{5}
\]
It remains to check the extra inequality defining \(A\). From the lower middle-divisor inequality and \(c=2^bd\),
\[
2^a m=n\le 2c^2=2^{2b+1}d^2.
\]
Since \(b\le a\), this implies
\[
2^a m\le 2^{2a+1}d^2
       =2^a\bigl(2^{a+1}d^2\bigr).
\]
Cancelling the positive factor \(2^a\) yields
\[
m\le 2^{a+1}d^2. \tag{6}
\]
Together with (5), this proves \(d\in A\). Thus taking the odd part defines a map
\[
\phi:M\longrightarrow A,
\qquad \phi(2^bd)=d.
\]

We next prove that \(\phi\) is injective. Suppose two middle divisors \(c_1,c_2\) have the same odd part \(d\). Write
\[
c_1=2^{b_1}d,\qquad c_2=2^{b_2}d.
\]
If \(b_1<b_2\), then \(b_2\ge b_1+1\), so \(c_2\ge 2c_1\), and hence
\[
c_2^2\ge 4c_1^2. \tag{7}
\]
On the other hand, because both numbers are middle divisors,
\[
n\le 2c_1^2
\quad\text{and}\quad
c_2^2<2n.
\]
These inequalities imply
\[
c_2^2<2n\le 4c_1^2,
\]
contradicting (7). The case \(b_2<b_1\) is symmetric. Thus \(b_1=b_2\), and consequently \(c_1=c_2\). This proves injectivity.

To prove surjectivity, take \(d\in A\). Then \(d\) is an odd divisor of \(n\), hence \(d\mid m\), and
\[
d^2<2n,\qquad m\le 2^{a+1}d^2. \tag{8}
\]
We seek a power \(2^b\) such that \(c=2^bd\) is a middle divisor. There is at least one exponent \(b\) satisfying the lower middle inequality
\[
n\le 2(2^b)^2d^2, \tag{9}
\]
because \(b=a\) works: by (8),
\[
n=2^am
 \le 2^a\cdot 2^{a+1}d^2
 =2^{2a+1}d^2
 =2(2^a)^2d^2.
\]
Let \(b_0\) be the least nonnegative integer for which (9) holds. Since \(a\) is one such exponent, \(b_0\le a\). Therefore
\[
c=2^{b_0}d
\]
divides \(2^am=n\), because \(d\mid m\). By the choice of \(b_0\), it also satisfies
\[
n\le 2c^2. \tag{10}
\]
We must establish the strict upper inequality \(c^2<2n\). There are two cases.

If \(b_0=0\), then \(c=d\), and \(c^2=d^2<2n\) is already part of (8).

If \(b_0>0\), minimality says that \(b_0-1\) does not satisfy (9). Hence
\[
2(2^{b_0-1})^2d^2<n. \tag{11}
\]
Since \(2^{b_0}=2\cdot 2^{b_0-1}\), we have
\[
c^2=(2^{b_0}d)^2
=4(2^{b_0-1})^2d^2
=2\bigl(2(2^{b_0-1})^2d^2\bigr).
\]
Doubling (11) therefore gives \(c^2<2n\). In either case, together with (10), \(c\in M\). Since \(d\) is odd, removing the full power of \(2\) from \(c=2^{b_0}d\) returns exactly \(d\). Thus every element of \(A\) has a preimage under \(\phi\), proving that \(\phi\) is surjective. We have therefore shown
\[
|A|=|M|. \tag{12}
\]

It remains to relate \(B\) and \(G\). Every member of either set is an odd divisor of \(n\), hence a divisor of the odd part \(m\). For a divisor \(d\mid m\), let
\[
\psi(d)=\frac{m}{d}.
\]
Complementary divisors of \(m\) are paired by this operation: if \(d\mid m\), then \(m/d\mid m\) and
\[
\frac{m}{m/d}=d.
\]
Thus \(\psi\) is an involution on the divisors of \(m\). We show that it carries \(B\) exactly onto \(G\).

Take \(d\in B\), and put \(e=m/d\). Then \(d,e>0\), \(de=m\), and both are odd divisors of \(n\). The defining extra inequality for \(B\) is
\[
2^{a+1}d^2<m=de.
\]
Cancelling the positive factor \(d\) gives
\[
2^{a+1}d<e. \tag{13}
\]
Multiplying (13) by the positive number \(e\), and using \(de=m\) and (1), gives
\[
2n=2^{a+1}m
   =2^{a+1}de
   <e^2.
\]
Therefore \(e\in G\). This shows that \(\psi\) maps \(B\) into \(G\).

Conversely, take \(e\in G\), and put \(d=m/e\). Again \(d,e>0\), \(de=m\), and \(d\) is an odd divisor of \(n\). Since \(e\in G\),
\[
2n<e^2.
\]
Using (1) and \(m=ed\), this becomes
\[
2^{a+1}ed<e^2.
\]
Cancelling the positive factor \(e\) yields
\[
2^{a+1}d<e.
\]
Multiplying by \(d>0\), we obtain
\[
2^{a+1}d^2<ed=m. \tag{14}
\]
This is the extra inequality required for membership in \(B\). We also need the inequality \(d^2<2n\), since \(B\subseteq L\). Because \(a+1\ge 1\), we have \(2^{a+1}>1\). From (14),
\[
d^2\le 2^{a+1}d^2<m.
\]
Also, by (1),
\[
m<2^{a+1}m=2n,
\]
since \(m>0\) and \(2^{a+1}>1\). Hence \(d^2<2n\), as required. Thus \(d\in B\).

The operation \(d\mapsto m/d\) is its own inverse on divisors of \(m\), so the two preceding directions establish a bijection between \(B\) and \(G\). Consequently,
\[
|B|=|G|. \tag{15}
\]

Combining (4), (12), and (15), we obtain the promised second identity
\[
|L|=|A|+|B|=|M|+|G|,
\]
which is (3).

Finally, substitute (2) and (3):
\[
|O|-|M|
=(|L|+|G|)-|M|
=(|M|+|G|+|G|)-|M|
=2|G|.
\]
By the definitions of \(O\), \(M\), and \(G\), this says that the number of odd divisors of \(n\) minus the number of middle divisors of \(n\) is twice the number of odd divisors of \(n\) greater than \(\sqrt{2n}\), as claimed.
